vignette:
The Weight of What She Carried Home

Mei Lin is forty-nine years old, and she carries herself with the kind of careful stillness that people sometimes mistake for calm. She sits in the chair across from the desk with her hands folded in her lap, her posture precise, as though she has spent years practicing how to take up exactly the right amount of space — no more, no less.

She served as a military communications technician in a regional conflict zone in her late twenties, deployed alongside a multinational peacekeeping force. She was not supposed to be in combat. That is what she says, almost reflexively, whenever she begins to talk about it — I was not supposed to be there. But the convoy she was traveling with came under sustained fire one afternoon on a dirt road outside a village whose name she still cannot say aloud. She watched two soldiers die within arm's reach of her. She held one of them. She remembers the specific quality of the light, the smell of burning metal, and the sound her own voice made when she screamed for help that did not come quickly enough.

She returned home, married, had a son, and told almost no one what had happened. For years, the strategy worked well enough. She built a career in IT support, where the problems are concrete and solvable — a crashed system, a misconfigured network, a user locked out of their account. She is good at her job. Her colleagues describe her as methodical and reliable. She likes the logic of it, the way a problem either resolves or it doesn't, the way there is always a traceable cause.

Her marriage ended seven years ago. Her ex-husband described her as emotionally unavailable, which she does not entirely dispute. She knew, even then, that something in her had been walled off. She just believed the wall was necessary.

What brought her in now, at forty-nine, is a system migration project at work. For three weeks, she has been troubleshooting a server room that overheated and triggered the building's fire suppression system. The sudden hiss of the discharge, the alarm, the acrid smell — her body responded before her mind could intervene. She found herself crouched behind a server rack, heart hammering, convinced with absolute certainty that she was back on that road. A younger colleague found her there and asked if she was all right, and the shame of that moment seems to pain her almost as much as the episode itself.

She has not been sleeping. When she does sleep, she wakes at two or three in the morning with her pulse elevated and the sheets damp, fragments of the convoy still vivid and immediate. During the day she moves through a persistent low-grade vigilance that exhausts her — scanning parking garages, sitting with her back to walls, flinching at car doors slamming in the street below her apartment window. She has started driving a longer route to work to avoid a road construction site where the jackhammers sound, she says, too much like that.

She describes a persistent sense of numbness around her son, now in his early twenties, that troubles her deeply. She loves him — she says this firmly, wanting it understood — but there is a glass wall between the feeling and her ability to express it. She worries he has grown up with a mother who was present in every practical sense and absent in the ways that matter most.

What is striking about Mei Lin is not the severity of what she describes but the decades of functional endurance that preceded this moment. She managed. She adapted. She built a life with careful, deliberate hands around something she never looked at directly. Now, at forty-nine, the thing she has been managing has begun, quietly and insistently, to demand her attention.
